name: Achaemenid Persia
capital: Pasargadae, Susa, Babylon, Ecbatana; ceremonial capital Persepolis
summary: Founded by Cyrus the Great, the largest empire the world had yet seen, known for royal roads, satrapies and tolerance of local customs.

knownFor.label: Royal Road
knownFor.note: A 2,500 km road with relay stations for royal messengers.

knownFor.label: Persepolis
knownFor.note: Ceremonial capital with carved reliefs of tribute bearers.

knownFor.label: Immortals
knownFor.note: An elite infantry unit kept at 10,000 men.

knownFor.label: Cyrus Cylinder
knownFor.note: A royal declaration often linked to tolerance of local religions.

location.value: Based on the Iranian plateau (Persis). At its height it stretched from the Balkans and Cyrenaica (Libya) to the Indus Valley, including Anatolia, Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Levant and much of Central Asia.

terrain.value: Mountains and plateaus in Iran, fertile river valleys (Mesopotamia, Nile, Indus), and deserts in between, linked by royal roads.

climate.value: Arid to semi-arid in the core. Underground irrigation channels (qanats) watered the plateau.
climate.source: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (2002)

resources.value: The wealth of conquered Egypt, Babylonia, Lydia and India: grain, silver, gold, and tribute in kind.

disasters.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

population.value: About 17–35 million around 500 BCE (Wikipedia infobox). By some estimates this was a large share of the world’s population at the time.

urbanisation.value: Major cities: Babylon, Susa, Ecbatana, Sardis, Memphis, and the ceremonial capitals Pasargadae and Persepolis.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Achaemenid Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Capital cities (checked 9 Nov 2026)

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Cyrus allowed exiled peoples, including the Judeans, to return home (538 BCE). Deported and resettled groups worked on royal projects.

economicBase.value: Agriculture across many provinces, plus trade and tribute paid by each satrapy (province).

tradeRoutes.value: The Royal Road from Susa to Sardis (about 2,500 km), with relay stations. Couriers could cover it in about a week. Sea routes in the Persian Gulf and Mediterranean.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate exists. Its treasuries held vast silver and gold, much of it later seized by Alexander.

moneyAndTax.value: Darius I introduced the gold daric and silver siglos coins. Each satrapy paid fixed tribute (e.g. Babylon about 1,000 silver talents a year, according to Herodotus).

inequality.value: The Persian king and nobility, local elites in each province, farmers, and workers including dependants and slaves.
inequality.source: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (2002)

governmentType.value: A monarchy ruled by the “King of Kings”, with a centralised bureaucracy and provinces (satrapies) run by governors (satraps), military commanders and secretaries.

keyRulers.value: Cyrus the Great (559–530 BCE). Cambyses II (530–522). Darius the Great (522–486). Xerxes I (486–465). Artaxerxes I (465–424). Darius III (336–330, last).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Achaemenid Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); Britannica: Achaemenian dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Hereditary, but often violent: Darius I took power in 522 BCE after killing a ruler he said was the impostor Gaumata (accounts differ). Several kings were murdered by courtiers.

institutions.value: About 20–30 satrapies, the Royal Road and postal system, Aramaic as the common administrative language, and a codified royal law (data). The Persepolis archives hold over 10,000 administrative tablets.

stability.value: Revolts after 522 BCE (recorded in the Behistun inscription). Babylonian revolts (484 BCE). The Great Satraps’ Revolt (372–362 BCE). Egypt broke away (404–343 BCE).

eliteConflict.value: Court plots: Xerxes I was assassinated (465 BCE), and the eunuch Bagoas poisoned Artaxerxes III (338 BCE) before being forced to drink poison himself.

armyAndTech.value: A large professional army and navy. The elite “Immortals” guard of 10,000. Contingents from many subject peoples. Darius I founded a royal navy.

majorWars.value: Conquest of Media (550), Lydia (547), Babylonia (539) and Egypt (525 BCE). The Greco-Persian Wars (499–449 BCE: Marathon 490, Salamis 480, Plataea 479). Alexander’s invasion (Issus 333, Gaugamela 331 BCE).

territoryChange.value: Peak extent about 5.5 million km² under Darius I (around 500 BCE). Repulsed from Scythia (513 BCE) and Greece (490, 480–479 BCE).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Greek city-states (Athens, Sparta), Egypt, the Scythians, and Macedon. It also funded Greek rivalries, e.g. backing Sparta.

inventions.value: The Royal Road and relay postal system, qanat irrigation, and a large-scale imperial bureaucracy that later empires copied.

scienceEducation.value: Scribes kept administrative records in Elamite and Aramaic. Royal inscriptions in Old Persian cuneiform.

openness.value: Notably multicultural and religiously tolerant (especially under Cyrus), working through local elites and customs.

communicationTransport.value: The Royal Road (about 2,700 km) from Sardis to Susa, with relay stations; mounted couriers could cover it in about nine days.

religion.value: Zoroastrianism was the religion of the kings (Wikipedia’s infobox calls it the state religion; the body marks this as needing a citation). Babylonian, Jewish, Egyptian, Greek and other religions were tolerated.

languageWriting.value: Old Persian (dynastic, in cuneiform) and Imperial Aramaic (the common administrative language), plus Elamite, Akkadian, Greek and others.

artsArchitecture.value: Persepolis with its reliefs of tribute-bearers, Pasargadae, the tomb of Cyrus, and the Behistun inscription.

socialStructure.value: King and Persian nobility, satraps, local elites, soldiers, farmers, craftsmen and slaves (private slave sales were taxed).

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Achaemenid king, whose inscriptions celebrated the diversity of subject peoples under his rule.
sharedIdentity.source: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (2002)

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick homes for most people; bread, dates, figs, wine and meat for the rich; trousers and long robes.

neighbours.value: Greek city-states, Macedon, the Scythians, Egypt, Nubia, Arabia and Indian kingdoms.

ideasReligions.value: Its bureaucracy and postal system were adopted by later Hellenistic, Roman and Islamic empires. Cyrus is honoured in the Hebrew Bible for freeing the Judeans.

colonisation.value: A conquering empire that ruled many peoples through satraps, while generally keeping local institutions and religions.

riseSignals.value: Cyrus united the Persians and Medes, then quickly defeated Lydia and Babylon. Flexible, tolerant rule kept conquered elites loyal.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Darius the Great (522–486 BCE): greatest extent and the organisation of the empire.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Achaemenid Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026); Britannica: Achaemenian dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: Defeats in Greece, revolts by satraps and in Egypt, court murders and succession crises. Historians now question the old Greek picture of a “decadent” Persia.

outcome.value: Conquered by Alexander the Great (334–330 BCE). Its lands passed to the Macedonian successor kingdoms, especially the Seleucids and Ptolemies. An Iranian empire returned with the Parthians.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Achaemenid Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026); Britannica: Achaemenian dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Royal inscriptions (Behistun), the Persepolis tablets, Babylonian records, archaeology, the Hebrew Bible, and Greek historians (Herodotus, Xenophon), who were often hostile. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Briant (2002).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Much comes from Greek enemies. Darius’ succession, the role of Zoroastrianism and population figures are debated. The founding is dated 559 BCE (Cyrus becomes king) or 550 BCE (empire). Britannica (checked 9 Nov 2026) dates the dynasty 559–330 BCE from Cyrus II, gives its widest reach under Darius I and Xerxes I, and ends it with the death of Darius III after his defeat by Alexander (330 BCE).
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Achaemenid Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026); Britannica: Achaemenian dynasty (checked 9 Nov 2026)
